1.pericope_label: O ye children of Benjamin, gather yourselves to flee out of the midst of Jerusalem, and blow the trumpet in Tekoa, and set up a sign of fire in Beth–haccerem: for evil appeareth out of the north, and great destruction. I have likened the daughter of Zion to a comely and delicate woman. The shepherds with their flocks shall come unto her; they shall pitch their tents against her round about; they shall feed every one in his place.

schools.summary: Fix the signals on the map, deny that the word rendered comely means a woman at all, and reject a proposed identification of the shepherds with a nomad swarm.
Explain why punishment is set before the eyes rather than merely announced, and account for the pastoral idiom from the prophet's upbringing.
Set the scene in the prophet's vision and identify the places and the invaders plainly.
Stresses the security the alarm interrupts, the city seeing no cloud gathering.

debates.question: To what is the daughter of Zion likened?

positions.position: To a woman dwelling at home in ease, though others supply land or pasture, and a third rendering makes it a vocative followed by I have destroyed.
Not to a woman at all, the word being absent from the Hebrew and the term rendered comely elsewhere translated fold or habitation, so probably to a fair pasturage.
Doubtful whether a tender maid is meant or something else.

debates.question: Why are the children of Benjamin addressed?

positions.position: The tribe stayed with Judah at the revolt, part of the city lay in its territory, and the prophet was born within it.
The city stood on the border of the two, the northern walls lying in Benjamin.
The prophet mentions them as his own countrymen.
He addresses his own kindred first.

outliers.claim: Rejects one scholar's suggestion that the shepherds and flocks point to a nomad swarm or a particular northern people, making them princes who with their peoples besiege and sack the city.

themes: O ye children of Benjamin, gather yourselves to flee out of the midst of Jerusalem, and blow the trumpet in Tekoa, and set up a sign of fire in Beth–haccerem: for evil appeareth out of the north, and great destruction.
I have likened the daughter of Zion to a comely and delicate woman.
The shepherds with their flocks shall come unto her; they shall pitch their tents against her round about; they shall feed every one in his place.

4.pericope_label: Prepare ye war against her; arise, and let us go up at noon. Woe unto us! for the day goeth away, for the shadows of the evening are stretched out. Arise, and let us go by night, and let us destroy her palaces.

schools.summary: Correct prepare to sanctify, since a battle opened with sacrifices and divinations, and describe the transition from figure to reality.
Count the hours of the day to explain the complaint that it fails, and mark where the similitude of shepherds is dropped.
Read the words as the invaders' own impatience, or as God's summons that they are eager to obey.

debates.question: Who speaks the summons to war?

positions.position: Either the Lord calling the Chaldeans or the invaders stirring one another up, the latter preferable on what follows.
God's own summons, the eagerness showing how ready they are to obey.
The invaders, impatient lest the besieged gain leisure to strengthen themselves.
The soldiers of the invading army, so eager that they will not rest at noon for their meal.
The Chaldeans, introduced by personification as encouraging one another.

outliers.claim: Counts the hours to fix the sense: from midday to nightfall is six hours, the day divided into twelve beginning at sunrise, so the meaning is that since the city cannot be taken in six hours they will attack by night.
Explains the consecration of the war as undertaken because the campaign was under commission from God.

themes: Prepare ye war against her; arise, and let us go up at noon. Woe unto us! for the day goeth away, for the shadows of the evening are stretched out.
Arise, and let us go by night, and let us destroy her palaces.

6.pericope_label: For thus hath the Lord of hosts said, Hew ye down trees, and cast a mount against Jerusalem: this is the city to be visited; she is wholly oppression in the midst of her. As a fountain casteth out her waters, so she casteth out her wickedness: violence and spoil is heard in her; before me continually is grief and wounds. Be thou instructed, O Jerusalem, lest my soul depart from thee; lest I make thee desolate, a land not inhabited.

schools.summary: Describe the siege works from the Assyrian reliefs and find two difficulties in the Hebrew of the fountain clause.
Names the two things needing to be done, exposing the people's stupidity and making them know they had to do with God and not the Chaldeans.
Read the siege works as timber for machines and a mound for the engines, and say plainly that there is still respite.

debates.question: What does the clause about the fountain mean?

positions.position: Wickedness poured out in abundance and continually.
The inhabitants are incessant in their acts of iniquity and do nothing but sin.
The word rendered fountain is better a cistern, is oddly pointed, and the verb's etymology is uncertain, so it has been rendered as gathering, keeping in, keeping cool, or letting flow.
An amplification of the charge that the city was a den of thieves: many vices may break out and repentance follow, but these heap vices on vices.

outliers.claim: Calls the word for departing a most emphatic metaphor, by which God expresses how great a grief it is to withdraw, like separating one limb from another.
Says plainly that there is still respite: a wholehearted return even now would arrest the advancing army on its march and turn it back.

themes: For thus hath the Lord of hosts said, Hew ye down trees, and cast a mount against Jerusalem: this is the city to be visited; she is wholly oppression in the midst of her.
As a fountain casteth out her waters, so she casteth out her wickedness: violence and spoil is heard in her; before me continually is grief and wounds.
Be thou instructed, O Jerusalem, lest my soul depart from thee; lest I make thee desolate, a land not inhabited.

9.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord of hosts, They shall throughly glean the remnant of Israel as a vine: turn back thine hand as a grapegatherer into the baskets. To whom shall I speak, and give warning, that they may hear? behold, their ear is uncircumcised, and they cannot hearken: behold, the word of the Lord is unto them a reproach; they have no delight in it.

schools.summary: Read the grape-gatherer's last tendril as a parable of unsparing desolation, and resolve the prophet's despairing question as compulsion he cannot escape.
Insist that the verb means to glean after the vintage rather than to gather it, and reconcile the despair with the earlier offer of reconciliation.
Address the gleaning to the invaders and press the repeated returns for spoil.
Describes the havoc as the enemy quartering long among them, insatiable after blood and treasure.

debates.question: How can the prophet despair after being told God is still ready to be reconciled?

positions.position: He despairs of any success by his ministry, the people so depraved that speaking is beating the air.
There is nothing inconsistent: he wished so far as he could to secure their safety, and asks as of something unexpected.
He might warn once more to turn the judgment away, but they are utterly hardened; yet he cannot be silent, being filled with the fury of God.
He has heard the message but asks who will listen, the ear being uncircumcised as though never brought into covenant.

outliers.claim: Distinguishes the figures: an uncircumcised ear signifies the rejecting of instruction and an uncircumcised heart an obstinate will, and they had brought the incapacity on themselves by their own wilfulness.
Reads the gleaning as addressed to the invaders, to turn back and glean the remnant left after the capture, since even that remnant did not profit by the judgments.

themes: Thus saith the Lord of hosts, They shall throughly glean the remnant of Israel as a vine: turn back thine hand as a grapegatherer into the baskets.

To whom shall I speak, and give warning, that they may hear? behold, their ear is uncircumcised, and they cannot hearken: behold, the word of the Lord is unto them a reproach; they have no delight in it.

11.pericope_label: Therefore I am full of the fury of the Lord; I am weary with holding in: I will pour it out upon the children abroad, and upon the assembly of young men together: for even the husband with the wife shall be taken, the aged with him that is full of days. And their houses shall be turned unto others, with their fields and wives together: for I will stretch out my hand upon the inhabitants of the land, saith the Lord. For from the least of them even unto the greatest of them every one is given to covetousness; and from the prophet even unto the priest every one dealeth falsely.

schools.summary: Take the pouring out as a command from God's mouth rather than the prophet's resolve, and single out the two orders that should have checked the evil as foremost in promoting it.
Allow the fury to be read passively or actively, and explain why the loss of the land struck at the people's deepest confidence.
Read the fire of wrath as a burden that must be discharged, and gloss the falsehood as the proper sin of priests and prophets.

debates.question: Whose fury is the prophet full of?

positions.position: Either zeal for God's name or, following the Targum, the prophecy concerning the wrath to come.
Passively or actively: either indignant with holy zeal for God's cause, or dreading the judgment the Jews ignored.
The burden of a dreadful revelation he had endeavoured to suppress.
A righteous wrath filling a frail vessel and refusing to be controlled, though the next clause is better a command, pour it out.
The fire of God's wrath, which he must discharge.

outliers.claim: Explains the confidence the threat destroys: because it had been said this is my rest for ever, they thought their dwelling in the land as certain as the sun and moon in the heavens.
Reads the transfer of houses and fields as the result of being taken rather than a fresh charge.

themes: Therefore I am full of the fury of the Lord; I am weary with holding in: I will pour it out upon the children abroad, and upon the assembly of young men together: for even the husband with the wife shall be taken, the aged with him that is full of days.
And their houses shall be turned unto others, with their fields and wives together: for I will stretch out my hand upon the inhabitants of the land, saith the Lord.
For from the least of them even unto the greatest of them every one is given to covetousness; and from the prophet even unto the priest every one dealeth falsely.

14.pericope_label: They have healed also the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace. Were they ashamed when they had committed abomination? nay, they were not at all ashamed, neither could they blush: therefore they shall fall among them that fall: at the time that I visit them they shall be cast down, saith the Lord. Thus saith the Lord, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.

schools.summary: Correct the shame clause to an assertion rather than a question, and render the old paths as the eternal paths, beyond the mere antiquity of the nation's life.
Restrict the slight healing to prophets and priests, and deny that the fault can be extenuated as ignorance.
Turn the crossroads into a narrative of a traveller who asks directions, and note the textual status of two words.

debates.question: What is the force of the shame clause?

positions.position: The Hebrew gives an assertion, not a question: they are brought to shame, and yet were not ashamed, having lost the power to blush.
Referred first to the false prophets and priests, not ashamed when reproved, being given up to judicial hardness.
The address widens here to the whole people, whose disgrace is visible to heaven and earth yet touches them with no shame.
They sinned by encouraging the people and joining them.

outliers.claim: Tells the crossroads as a narrative of a traveller who stops, cannot fix his choice, meets another, gets directions and arrives, and notes that an excellent sermon on the words stands among the tales of the first English poet.
States the doctrinal point: judgment cannot be turned aside by sacrifice without a change of heart.

themes: They have healed also the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace.

Were they ashamed when they had committed abomination? nay, they were not at all ashamed, neither could they blush: therefore they shall fall among them that fall: at the time that I visit them they shall be cast down, saith the Lord.
Thus saith the Lord, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.

17.pericope_label: Also I set watchmen over you, saying, Hearken to the sound of the trumpet. But they said, We will not hearken. Therefore hear, ye nations, and know, O congregation, what is among them. Hear, O earth: behold, I will bring evil upon this people, even the fruit of their thoughts, because they have not hearkened unto my words, nor to my law, but rejected it.

schools.summary: Ground the watchmen in scriptural usage or in military practice, and say plainly that the clause addressed to the congregation is far from clear.
Explain why the trumpet aggravates the charge, and why the address turns outward to the earth at all.
Identify the watchmen as prophets sent to warn and the trumpet as the prophet's loud crying.
Reads the appeal as one to the equity of the proceedings, addressed to the great men of the nations.

positions.position: Prophets, per two Jewish commentators, and teachers per the Targum, extending to the apostles and all faithful preachers.
Prophets sent to warn.
Those who stand on the watch-tower to keep a lookout and proclaim what they have seen in spirit.
The sentinels of an army, giving the signal not for advance but for retreat.

outliers.claim: Explains why the trumpet aggravates the charge: it ought to have penetrated their minds more than anything, being louder than any human voice and not commonly heard except when war is at hand.
Says the nations are called as spectators of the severity, the greatness of the punishment answering the greatness of the sins.

themes: Also I set watchmen over you, saying, Hearken to the sound of the trumpet. But they said, We will not hearken.
Therefore hear, ye nations, and know, O congregation, what is among them.
Hear, O earth: behold, I will bring evil upon this people, even the fruit of their thoughts, because they have not hearkened unto my words, nor to my law, but rejected it.

20.pericope_label: To what purpose cometh there to me incense from Sheba, and the sweet cane from a far country? your burnt offerings are not acceptable, nor your sacrifices sweet unto me. Therefore thus saith the Lord, Behold, I will lay stumblingblocks before this people, and the fathers and the sons together shall fall upon them; the neighbour and his friend shall perish.

schools.summary: Locate the incense country and its literary fame, and correct the stumbling-block clause so that the pairs become the subjects of the second verb.
Answer the hypocrites who thought incense made expiation, and compare the coming judgments to nets that leave no escape.
Identify the sweet cane with the aromatic calamus of the anointing oil and put the question of its purpose bluntly.

positions.position: The inroads of the enemies whose formidableness the next verse depicts.
Nets or traps, met wherever they go, so that however they conspire they suffer the same punishment.
Things God suffers to be laid in their way as the occasion of their destruction.
Better rendered, I give unto this people stumbling-blocks, and they shall stumble over them.
Laid because of their immorality and hypocrisy and their confidence in legal rites.

outliers.claim: Identifies the sweet cane as the aromatic calamus, which yields a fine smell when dried and pulverised and was used in making the holy anointing oil.

themes: To what purpose cometh there to me incense from Sheba, and the sweet cane from a far country? your burnt offerings are not acceptable, nor your sacrifices sweet unto me.
Therefore thus saith the Lord, Behold, I will lay stumblingblocks before this people, and the fathers and the sons together shall fall upon them; the neighbour and his friend shall perish.

22.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord, Behold, a people cometh from the north country, and a great nation shall be raised from the sides of the earth. They shall lay hold on bow and spear; they are cruel, and have no mercy; their voice roareth like the sea; and they ride upon horses, set in array as men for war against thee, O daughter of Zion.

schools.summary: Allow a Scythian as well as a Chaldean reference, render the verb as roused, and supply the evidence for the invaders' exceptional ferocity.
Defend the repeated introductory formula and reject the rendering of the second weapon as a shield.
Name the Chaldeans without hesitation and gloss the sides of the earth as the uttermost parts of their territories.

debates.question: Is the second weapon a spear or a shield?

positions.position: A spear, since each was furnished to fight near and afar off, though the Targum renders shields.
Not a shield: those who so render it miss the design, since no defence is in view but shooting at a distance; three versions render it improperly.
A javelin, shot or hurled, the special weapon of the Chaldeans.

outliers.claim: Supplies the evidence for the invaders' exceptional ferocity, prisoners impaled or flayed alive or burnt in the furnace being common incidents of their wars, and notes that cavalry appears to have been a novelty to a people used to war-chariots.
Reports a scholar's identification of the invaders as Scythians, who had overrun many parts of Asia and spread consternation wherever their name was heard.

themes: Thus saith the Lord, Behold, a people cometh from the north country, and a great nation shall be raised from the sides of the earth.
They shall lay hold on bow and spear; they are cruel, and have no mercy; their voice roareth like the sea; and they ride upon horses, set in array as men for war against thee, O daughter of Zion.

24.pericope_label: We have heard the fame thereof: our hands wax feeble: anguish hath taken hold of us, and pain, as of a woman in travail. Go not forth into the field, nor walk by the way; for the sword of the enemy and fear is on every side. O daughter of my people, gird thee with sackcloth, and wallow thyself in ashes: make thee mourning, as for an only son, most bitter lamentation: for the spoiler shall suddenly come upon us. I have set thee for a tower and a fortress among my people, that thou mayest know and try their way.

schools.summary: Call the tower verse difficult, its words found nowhere else, and prefer a prover of ore on the recent commentators' authority; distinguish sprinkling ashes from wallowing in them.
Argue from word order that the first term must be a citadel, since the word for fortress follows.
Describe the assayer's cupel in detail, and alone read the verse as encouragement to the prophet rather than a description of his office.

debates.question: Is the prophet set as a tower or as an assayer?

positions.position: Either a watch-tower or a trier, the latter likelier since the metaphor is carried on afterwards.
A prover of ore, on the authority of the most recent commentators, which agrees with the metallurgical imagery following.
A citadel for watching: since the word for fortress follows, the first term can only be a rampart.
Appointed to make an assay, the process being that of the cupel, which absorbs the lead and with it the dross.
A fortified tower given for the prophet's own safety and encouragement.

outliers.claim: Observes that the words fear on every side impressed themselves on the prophet's mind and became a watchword, so that he later gave them as a name to a particular man.

themes: We have heard the fame thereof: our hands wax feeble: anguish hath taken hold of us, and pain, as of a woman in travail.
Go not forth into the field, nor walk by the way; for the sword of the enemy and fear is on every side.
O daughter of my people, gird thee with sackcloth, and wallow thyself in ashes: make thee mourning, as for an only son, most bitter lamentation: for the spoiler shall suddenly come upon us.
I have set thee for a tower and a fortress among my people, that thou mayest know and try their way.

28.pericope_label: They are all grievous revolters, walking with slanders: they are brass and iron; they are all corrupters. The bellows are burned, the lead is consumed of the fire; the founder melteth in vain: for the wicked are not plucked away. Reprobate silver shall men call them, because the Lord hath rejected them.

schools.summary: Render the verdict as rebels of rebels, offer a different construction of the bellows, and note that the adjective and verb of the last clause share a root.
Explain why the verdict is withheld until now, and close on the concession the word silver involves.
Take the bellows for the prophets' spent breath and gloss refuse silver commercially.

debates.question: What do the burnt bellows represent?

positions.position: The prophet's own mouth and throat, dried and hoarse through reproving to no profit, per a Jewish commentator and the Targum.
The same reading, which interpreters generally give, the mouth being the bellows by which the fire was kindled.
The prophets' breath spent to no purpose and their strength consumed by their labour.
The life of the prophet filled with the breath of God, consumed by that blast and yet faulty in its work; and lead is the only outcome of their fire.
A long but resultless smelting that has brought no purification and no separation of the wicked.

outliers.claim: Explains why the verdict on the people is placed here rather than at the opening: said at first it would have kindled their fury or been treated with contempt, but coming as what God had known through his servant it had more weight.

themes: They are all grievous revolters, walking with slanders: they are brass and iron; they are all corrupters.
The bellows are burned, the lead is consumed of the fire; the founder melteth in vain: for the wicked are not plucked away.
Reprobate silver shall men call them, because the Lord hath rejected them.
